faq.answer: Because it wants every household able to cope with a few days of disruption: storms, floods, a power cut, a water supply failure or a cyber incident. Its July 2026 resilience report sets the backdrop: “new conflict in the Middle East, a growing number of sub-threshold attacks from Russia, the unprecedented growth of new technology, several major cyber attacks, and increasingly severe weather”. The ask is modest and not new: a few days of water, food that needs no cooking, a torch, a radio and a power bank. It is not a warning of war at home.

faq.question: Are UK households being urged to stock 9 key items immediately?
faq.answer: No minister has said that. faq.question: Is the government giving out free survival kits?
faq.answer: No. The government gives advice, not kits. GOV.UK Prepare, the official advice, asks households to “put together an emergency kit of items at home”, and suggests building it up over time rather than buying everything at once. The national campaign due later this autumn is advice too: the Cabinet Office describes it as “new advice for households on preparing for disruption and emergencies”. faq.question: How much water should I keep per person?
faq.answer: GOV.UK Prepare quotes the World Health Organisation’s survival minimum of 2.5 to 3 litres per person per day for drinking, and says about 10 litres a day is more comfortable once cooking and basic hygiene are included. For three days, the British Red Cross and Ready Scotland figure, that is roughly 9 litres of drinking water per person, or 30 litres to carry on more or less normally.

faq.question: How many days should I cover?
faq.answer: The official advice is built around a few days, which covers the great majority of UK disruption. A briefing about the coming government campaign, posted on 1 October by a Welsh charity, Glamorgan Voluntary Services, says it will ask households to build up three days of non-perishable food and bottled water over time, so a three-day figure may appear when it launches. That briefing is not published government guidance. Our own guides work through three days and two weeks, because two weeks is cheap once the shelf exists and covers a longer storm or supply problem.
